messages.content: Briefly describe the history of cannibalism in the United States

message.content:
The history of cannibalism in the United States is largely defined by extreme survival situations rather than cultural or ritualistic practices. Because cannibalism carries a profound social taboo, documented cases in American history are almost exclusively associated with desperate, life-or-death scenarios.

Here are the most notable instances and contexts:

### 1. The Donner Party (1846–1847)
The most famous instance of cannibalism in U.S. history occurred when a group of American pioneers traveling to California became trapped by heavy snow in the Sierra Nevada mountains. Of the 87 members of the party, nearly half died. Survivors were forced to consume the remains of the deceased to avoid starvation. The incident became a national sensation and remains a grim symbol of the perils of westward expansion.

### 2. The Alferd Packer Case (1874)
Alferd Packer, a prospector in the Colorado Territory, became the only American ever convicted of cannibalism. Packer led a group of five men into the San Juan Mountains during a harsh winter. He returned alone months later, appearing well-fed. He eventually confessed to killing his companions, claiming it was in self-defense and that he resorted to cannibalism only
